summary: Describes the Layered Coding Transport building block, which provides transport support for reliable content delivery and stream delivery protocols. It is designed for IP multicast but also works with unicast.

plainLanguage.summary: When one sender broadcasts a file to many, each receiver may miss pieces. This is a basic kit for sending in layers so everyone can get the whole thing.

questions: what is the lct header format
how does lct handle congestion control
subtitle: The common packet header for scalable one-to-many content and stream delivery over IP multicast.

tldr.problem: Sending the same content to a huge number of receivers needs a transport that does not depend on feedback from each receiver, yet still has to share bandwidth fairly with other traffic.
tldr.mechanism: LCT defines a packet header that identifies the session and object, carries opaque congestion control information and a codepoint for the payload coding, and can be extended with optional header extensions.
tldr.outcome: LCT is a building block, not a full protocol. Protocol designs combine it with a congestion control scheme and, optionally, forward error correction. It obsoletes the Experimental RFC 3451.

today: RFC 5651 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes the Experimental RFC 3451. It removed the Sender Current Time and Expected Residual Time header fields in favour of the EXT_TIME extension, and created an IANA registry of header extension types. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: What LCT Is For
sections.content:
Layered Coding Transport (LCT) provides transport-level support for reliable content delivery and stream delivery protocols. It is designed for IP multicast but also supports protocols that use unicast. It is compatible with congestion control that gives receivers multiple delivery rates, and with coding techniques that provide reliable delivery.

LCT is a building block in the sense of RFC 3048, a product of the IETF RMT working group. This Proposed Standard is based on, and backwards compatible with, the Experimental RFC 3451, updated with accumulated experience.
sections.plainLanguage: LCT is a toolkit piece for sending the same thing to lots of people at once, such as a TV show or a big file.

sections.title: Sessions, Channels and Objects
sections.content:
An LCT session is a set of logically grouped channels from a single sender, carrying packets for one or more objects. A channel is a sender plus an address the sender chose. A receiver joins a channel to start getting its packets and leaves to stop. A session comes from one sender because that is the right unit for regulating traffic with congestion control.

LCT deliberately avoids anything that is not massively scalable. It has no way for receivers to send information back to the sender, although protocols built on it may add one. It requires congestion control but does not choose one, because a bulk download may want to use all available bandwidth while a stream may prefer a steady rate.

With multicast, an Any-Source Multicast channel is the pair (S,G) of sender and group, and with Source-Specific Multicast the LCT channel simply is the SSM channel. The RFC says SSM has compelling security advantages over ASM for preventing denial-of-service attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: A session is one radio station. Its channels are different frequencies. You tune in to the ones your connection can handle and tune out when you have what you need.

sections.title: Layered Coding and Congestion Control
sections.content:
Congestion control that conforms to RFC 2357 MUST be used in every LCT session, and the traffic must not compete unfairly with flow-adaptive protocols such as TCP. With a multiple rate scheme, the sender sends at rates that do not depend on receivers, and each receiver adjusts by joining and leaving channels. With a single rate scheme, a session usually has one channel and the sender varies its rate based on feedback. The multiple rate scheme of RFC 3738 is RECOMMENDED.

Layered coding splits a coded stream into ordered layers so quality or transfer speed varies with how many layers a receiver gets. With Forward Error Correction (FEC), reconstructing an object depends only on how many different packets arrive, not on which ones. So a receiver can join more layers to finish sooner, with little or no feedback. RFC 3453 covers FEC use and RFC 5052 specifies some codecs.

A complete protocol instantiation built on LCT MUST include a compatible congestion control protocol. It MAY add scalable reliability, session control and security protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a sender dropping puzzle pieces on several conveyor belts. You grab from as many belts as you can keep up with. Because any sufficient set of pieces will do, you do not need to ask for a particular one.

sections.title: The LCT Header
sections.content:
Every packet sent to an LCT session MUST include an LCT header. Its size is variable and given by the 8-bit HDR_LEN field in 32-bit words. The first word holds the version (1 for this specification), flags C, S, O and H that set field lengths, the Close Session flag A and Close Object flag B, and an 8-bit Codepoint.

  • CCI: the Congestion Control Information is opaque and is 32, 64, 96 or 128 bits depending on C (0 to 3).
  • TSI: the Transport Session Identifier is 0, 16, 32 or 48 bits and, with the sender's IP address, uniquely identifies the session. If UDP is underneath, its 16-bit source port MAY serve as the TSI; if nothing underneath provides one, the TSI MUST be in the header.
  • TOI: the Transport Object Identifier says which object a packet belongs to, for example TOI=0 for a first file and TOI=1 for a second. It must be in every packet if a session carries more than one object.
  • Codepoint: an opaque value passed to the payload decoder, similar to the RTP Payload Type, with its meaning agreed out-of-band.

The close flags are only hints, not a completely reliable mechanism. Reserved bits are set to 0 by senders and ignored by receivers.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is the label on each parcel: which show it is from, which episode, how the contents are packed, and a notice if the show is about to end.

sections.title: Header Extensions and Timing
sections.content:
Optional or variable-size fields go in Header Extensions after the default header. The 8-bit Header Extension Type (HET) decides the format: values 0 to 127 are variable-length and carry a length field (HEL), while 128 to 255 are fixed at one 32-bit word. Unrecognized extensions are ignored by default, which lets backward-compatible enhancements be added without changing the version number. The whole LCT header cannot exceed 255 32-bit words.

Three are defined. EXT_NOP (HET 0) must be ignored. EXT_AUTH (HET 1) carries packet authentication whose format is outside this document, and senders are RECOMMENDED to provide some form of packet authentication. EXT_TIME (HET 2) carries timing: the Sender Current Time, the Expected Residual Time in seconds for the current object, and the Session Last Changed time.
sections.plainLanguage: If the parcel label has no room for something, you can staple on extra stickers. Stickers a receiver does not understand are just skipped.

sections.title: Sender and Receiver Behaviour
sections.content:
Before joining, a receiver MUST obtain a session description, usually out-of-band. It includes the sender IP address, the number of channels, their addresses and ports, the TSI, and enough information to identify the congestion control protocol and any packet authentication scheme. The RFC mentions formats such as SDP (RFC 4566) and announcement by SAP (RFC 2974).

The sender must implement the sender side of a congestion control scheme using the CCI field. A receiver that cannot implement the session's congestion control MUST NOT join. When the session has several channels, receivers initially join only a minimal set, possibly one, so they do not start at high data rates. Receivers should not assume a packet for a new object means no more packets are in flight for the previous one, since reordering can occur.

Two service models are described. In a push model, receivers join until they have enough packets to rebuild an object and then wait for the next. In an on-demand model, a popular update might be sent for several days so receivers can join at any time and leave once done.
sections.plainLanguage: You first need the program guide to know which stations to tune to. Then you start with one quiet station and add more only as your connection allows.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because LCT is only a building block, any protocol that uses it MUST address several vulnerabilities, for example with source authentication and content integrity mechanisms. The RFC lists these.

  • Forged or modified TSI and TOI values can starve or misdirect sessions and objects, or make receivers allocate resources for fake ones.
  • The close flags, SCT and ERT can be forged to make receivers think a session ended, or to de-synchronize their clocks.
  • Changing the Codepoint, Congestion Control field or payload can break reconstruction or push receivers to the wrong rate.

A wrong or malicious session description can leave receivers unable to receive or make them try to receive at too high a rate, so protocols must protect it as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone could forge a parcel label to confuse listeners or tell them the show is over. So the label needs to be signed so you know it is real.

fields.name: V
fields.desc: LCT version number; 1 for this specification.

fields.name: C
fields.desc: Sets the CCI length: 32, 64, 96 or 128 bits.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Number of full 32-bit words in the TSI.

fields.name: O
fields.desc: Number of full 32-bit words in the TOI.

fields.name: H
fields.desc: Half-word flag for TSI and TOI lengths.

fields.name: HDR_LEN
fields.desc: Total LCT header length in 32-bit words.

fields.name: Codepoint
fields.desc: Opaque identifier of the payload codec.

items.label: EXT_TIME
items.desc: Timing: sender current time, expected residual time, session last changed.
